title: Testing Medicines
objective: After this level you can explain how new medicines are tested before doctors use them.
summary: Medicines go from lab tests through Phases 1 to 3, then Phase 4 after approval. Placebos, random allocation and blinding separate a drug's real effect from chance and hope.

cards.headline: In 1948, sealed envelopes decided who got a new drug.
cards.body: Britain's Medical Research Council was testing streptomycin against tuberculosis. Doctors couldn't pick who got it: the choice came from random numbers hidden in sealed envelopes. It's widely regarded as the first randomized controlled trial. Why go to all that trouble?

cards.headline: From lab bench to pharmacy shelf

events.label: Lab and animal studies answer basic safety questions
20 to 100 people: is it safe, and at what dose?
Up to several hundred patients: does it work, what side effects?
300 to 3,000 patients over 1 to 4 years: does it work, any harms?
After approval: thousands more, still watched for safety

cards.headline: The fake pill that keeps trials honest
cards.body: In many trials, one group gets the medicine and another gets a placebo: an inactive substance that looks just like it. Why? People can feel better simply because they expect a treatment to help. That's the placebo effect. Comparing the two groups shows whether changes come from the treatment or from chance. If the pill and the placebo do equally well, the pill isn't the one doing the work.

cards.headline: Random and blind
cards.body: Back to 1948's envelopes. Allocating patients at random stops researchers from choosing, even unconsciously, who gets the new drug, a choice that could tilt the result. Blinding goes further. In a blind test, patients don't know whether they got the drug or the placebo; in a double-blind test, their doctors don't know either. Nobody's hopes get a vote.

mascot.line: If nobody knows who got the real pill, nobody can nudge the answer. Clever, and a little sneaky.

cards.headline: Testing medicines: explained
learned: Preclinical, then Phases 1, 2 and 3, then Phase 4
A placebo looks like the drug but does nothing
Random allocation and blinding keep results fair
1948 streptomycin trial: the first randomized controlled trial

questions.prompt: In the FDA's sequence of clinical-trial phases, what is Phase 1 mainly checking?

options.label: Whether it beats other drugs in thousands
Safety and the right dose, in 20 to 100 people
How it behaves in lab dishes only

questions.explanation: Phase 1 tests safety and dosage in a small group of 20 to 100 people.

questions.prompt: Why do many clinical trials give one group an inactive placebo instead of nothing at all?

options.label: To separate the drug's real effect from expectation and chance
To make the trial last longer
Because placebos cure most illnesses
options.rationale: The placebo effect is about expectation, not cures.

questions.explanation: People can improve just from expecting help. Comparing drug and placebo groups shows whether changes come from the drug or from chance.

questions.prompt: Level 9's Vesalius checked human bodies himself instead of trusting Galen's books. How do clinical trials follow the same idea?

options.label: They trust the most famous doctor's opinion
They skip human testing entirely
options.rationale: Human trials are the whole point.

options.label: They test the drug on people and compare results

questions.explanation: Vesalius relied on his own human dissections; trials likewise judge a medicine by comparing groups of people, not by reputation.
